subtitle: Spot the workplace conditions that drive burnout, hold workload conversations that lead to real change, and set up team practices that spread the load fairly and protect recovery time.
audience: For supervisors, team leads and staff who coordinate work in DHS and DSD. It supports team practice; staffing decisions, leave, accommodation and formal HR matters stay with the responsible office.

lessons.title: What drives burnout
objectives: Describe burnout as a response to chronic workplace stress, as the World Health Organization frames it.
Name the six areas of worklife that Christina Maslach and Michael Leiter link to burnout.
Explain why relying on the most reliable person is a common driver of uneven load.
Distinguish fixing the work from asking individuals to cope better.
lessons.teaching:
Burnout is mostly a work problem, not a personal one. The World Health Organization describes it as an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, with three dimensions: exhaustion, mental distance from or negative feelings about one's job, and reduced professional efficacy. It is not classified as a medical condition, and this course is not a way to assess anyone.

Christina Maslach and Michael Leiter, whose research on burnout spans decades and many human service settings, describe six areas of worklife where a poor match between people and their work raises the risk: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. A heavy workload matters, and so does having little say in how work is done, feeling unrecognized, being isolated, sensing that decisions are unfair or being asked to work against one's values.

One pattern shows up on many teams. When positions go unfilled, the work is spread across whoever is left, and the most reliable person catches the most. It feels efficient. Over time it concentrates the load on the people the team can least afford to lose.

Self-care advice has its place, and it cannot fix a workload problem. Supervisors and managers control assignments, deadlines and staffing requests. This course focuses on what they can change, and on how everyone can make the load visible.
lessons.keyPoint: Burnout grows from a poor match between people and their work. Fix the work, not just the worker.
lessons.example: Practice case: The supervisor's team lost two positions last year and the work stayed the same. Two people are on leave. A difficult new case comes in, the kind the case manager always handles well. The case manager is already covering more than anyone else.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor do?
choices: Give the case to the case manager, who handles these best.
Check the team's caseload tracker and offer the case to the person with the most room, with the case manager available to advise.
feedback: The case gets handled well, and the case manager's load grows again. The pattern continues.
This spreads the load and still uses the case manager's skill, without making it the case manager's case. It also builds skill across the team.
Generous, and it pulls the supervisor away from the supervising the team needs right now.
lessons.reflection: On your team, who catches the most when work piles up? How did that pattern start?
lessons.action: Look at the six areas of worklife. Pick the one that most affects your team right now and write one change within your control.

check.question: Which list matches the six areas of worklife in Maslach and Leiter's research?
check.correct: Workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values.
wrong: Sleep, exercise, nutrition, hobbies, family and rest.
Salary, benefits, title, office space, schedule and travel.
check.feedback: The six areas describe the match between people and their work. Personal habits and pay matter too, but the burnout research centers on these six areas of the work itself.

lessons.title: Workload conversations that lead to change
objectives: Name what you have observed without judging or diagnosing.
Turn a check-in toward one specific change.
Follow up so a conversation becomes a change.
Respect a colleague's privacy while still acting on workload.
lessons.teaching:
A workload conversation is useful when it ends in a change. Many end with "let me know if that changes," and nothing does. A short structure helps: say what you have noticed, ask what would help and agree on one thing.

Name what you have seen, not what you think it means. "I've noticed emails from you after 9 p.m. most nights this month" is an observation. "You seem burned out" is a judgment the other person may not share and does not need to defend. Observations keep the conversation about the work.

Then turn toward a change. "What's one thing we could take off your plate this month?" is easier to answer than "How can I help?" It invites a specific answer, and it shows the supervisor is ready to act. Agree on one change, and set a date to check whether it helped.

People decide what to share about their own lives. A supervisor does not need to know why someone is stretched to adjust their workload. If personal matters come up, listen, keep it private and point to support such as LifeMatters, the state Employee Assistance Program.
lessons.keyPoint: Say what you have noticed, ask for one thing to change and follow up on a set date.
lessons.example: Practice case: In a one-on-one, the case manager says, "I'm fine, it's just a busy season." The supervisor has seen emails sent late at night for most of the month.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor say?
choices: "Okay, let me know if that changes."
"I've noticed you're working late a lot. What's one thing we could take off your plate this month?"
"You need to take better care of yourself."
feedback: It respects the case manager's answer and leaves the real issue untouched.
It names what the supervisor has seen, without judgment, and turns the talk toward a change the supervisor can make.
Kind in intent, and it puts the problem back on the case manager.
lessons.reflection: When someone has asked you how you are doing at work, what made it easy or hard to give a real answer?
lessons.action: In your next one-on-one, ask "What's one thing we could take off your plate this month?" Write down what you agree to and the date you will check back.

check.question: Which opening is an observation rather than a judgment?
check.correct: "I've noticed emails from you after 9 p.m. most nights this month."
check.feedback: An observation describes what you saw. Judgments ask the other person to defend themselves and can shut the conversation down.

lessons.title: Team practices that spread the load and protect recovery
objectives: Make a team's workload visible so it can be shared fairly.
Set up a fair way to assign difficult or unexpected work.
Agree on team norms that protect recovery time.
Cross-train so knowledge does not sit with one person.
lessons.teaching:
A load you cannot see is hard to share. A simple shared view of caseloads, open tasks or coverage, updated weekly, lets a team see who has room. It also lets people say "I'm full" with facts instead of feelings.

Decide how hard or unexpected work gets assigned before it arrives. A rotation, or a rule that the person with the most room takes it with an experienced colleague advising, is fairer than whoever is fastest or most willing. Fairness is one of the six areas of worklife for a reason.

Protect recovery time as a team. Agree on when messages can wait until morning. Hold one meeting-free block each week. Plan coverage before someone goes on leave, not after. These norms work best when the supervisor follows them too.

Cross-train on purpose. When only one person knows how to handle a type of case, that person can never fully step away. Pairing that person with a colleague on the next few cases spreads both the knowledge and the load.
lessons.keyPoint: Make the load visible, decide in advance how hard work is assigned and protect recovery time as a team.
lessons.example: Practice case: The supervisor proposes a shared weekly view of caseloads. The new colleague worries it will be used to judge people who are slower. A colleague who has been on the team for years says nothing.
lessons.question: What is the best way for the supervisor to respond?
choices: Drop the idea to avoid conflict.
Explain that the view is for sharing work, not rating people, agree as a team on what it shows and invite the quieter colleague's view.
Introduce it anyway, since the supervisor has the authority.
feedback: The worry is useful information, and dropping the idea leaves the load invisible.
This takes the concern seriously, sets a clear purpose and makes room for a voice that has not been heard. The tool is more likely to be used well.
The supervisor may have the authority, and a tool imposed over a worry may be avoided or misused.
lessons.reflection: Which team habit most protects recovery time on your team now? Which one is missing?
lessons.action: Propose one team practice in your next meeting: a shared view of the load, a rotation for hard cases or a meeting-free block. Agree on how you will know if it helps.

check.question: Why decide in advance how difficult or unexpected work will be assigned?
check.correct: So assignments are fair and predictable, instead of falling on whoever is fastest or most willing.
wrong: So the supervisor never has to make judgment calls.
So the most experienced person always gets the hardest work.
check.feedback: A clear rule spreads the load fairly. Supervisors still use judgment, and experience can be shared through advising without concentrating the load.

lessons.title: Raising workload with your own manager
objectives: Describe a team's workload to a manager with facts and a specific request.
Avoid hiding risk to protect a team's image.
Offer clear choices a manager can act on.
Recognize that sustainable pace is a shared leadership responsibility.
lessons.teaching:
Supervisors often protect their teams by absorbing problems. "We're managing" sounds loyal. It also hides the risk from the person who could help.

A short, factual update gives a manager something to act on. What has changed, what is at risk and what you need. "Caseloads are up 30 percent and two people are out. Reports are now late. I need one of two things: a temporary reassignment from another unit, or approval to move the quarterly report deadline." Offering two choices makes it easier to say yes to one.

A long list of every problem is honest and hard to act on. Lead with the most important risk and the most useful request. Keep the rest ready if asked.

The U.S. Surgeon General's framework for workplace well-being puts worker voice at the center. Raising workload honestly is part of that voice. Managers and senior leaders control staffing, priorities and deadlines, so a sustainable pace is a shared leadership responsibility, not a test of how much a team can absorb.
lessons.keyPoint: Bring your manager what has changed, what is at risk and two choices they can act on.
lessons.example: Practice case: The program manager asks the supervisor how the team is doing. Caseloads are up 30 percent, two people are on leave and two reports are late.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor say?
choices: "Caseloads are up 30 percent and two people are out. I need one of two things from you."
Send the program manager a long email listing every problem.
feedback: It protects the team's image and hides the risk from the person who can help.
Clear facts and a specific ask give the program manager something to act on.
Honest, and hard to act on without a clear request.
lessons.reflection: What makes it hard to tell your own manager that the team is stretched? What would make it easier?
lessons.action: Draft a three-sentence update for your manager: what has changed, what is at risk and two choices you need them to consider.

check.question: Which update is most useful to a manager?
check.correct: "Caseloads are up 30 percent and two people are out. Could we borrow one person from another unit or move the quarterly report deadline?"
check.feedback: Facts and specific choices let a manager act. Understating hides the risk; overstating without detail is hard to act on.

image.caption: The supervisor and the program manager.

cards.back: An occupational phenomenon from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. Not a medical diagnosis.
Workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values.
Giving extra work to the most dependable person until the load concentrates on the people the team can least afford to lose.
"I've noticed emails after 9 p.m." rather than "You seem burned out."
A check-in question that invites a specific change the supervisor can make.
What has changed, what is at risk and two choices your manager can act on.

aid.heading: Spot the drivers
items: Workload: is it more than the time available?
Control: do people have a say in how work is done?
Reward and fairness: is effort noticed and shared fairly?
Community and values: are people connected and able to work in line with their values?

aid.heading: Workload conversation
items: Ask: what's one thing we could take off your plate this month?
Set a date to check back.

aid.heading: Team practices
items: A shared weekly view of the load, used for sharing work, not rating people.
A rule or rotation for hard or unexpected work.
After-hours and meeting-free norms the supervisor follows too.
Cross-training so knowledge does not sit with one person.

aid.heading: Update your manager
items: Two choices you need them to consider.
